Kampen Seminary
kahm'pən sem'i-ner-ee
n. (the Theological School of the Seceder churches at Kampen in Overijssel, opened 1854)
Dutch Kampen, the Hanseatic town on the IJssel; Latin seminarium, a seed-plot.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kampen Seminary, the Theological School at Kampen, was opened in December 1854 by the Christian Seceded Reformed Church to train its ministers. Before that the Seceders had prepared men privately in the homes of pastors such as Van Velzen, Brummelkamp, and Van Raalte, with uneven results and much strife between the different schools. The synod of 1854 placed training under the churches themselves rather than a university, and called its first teachers from among the Secession's ministers, including Simon van Velzen and Helenius de Cock. Herman Bavinck taught dogmatics there from 1883 to 1902 and wrote the first edition of his Reformed Dogmatics at Kampen, and Klaas Schilder later taught there. After the union of 1892 the school remained the churches' seminary alongside Kuyper's Free University, a distinction Kampen's defenders thought essential: ministers of the church should be trained by the church and accountable to it. The principle is Paul's charge to Timothy, “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2), and the pattern of Ezra's Levites, who “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education, and theology as divinity, the science of God and divine things.

expand to see more

SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed in the several branches of learning.

THEOL'OGY, n. Divinity; the science of God and divine things; or the science which teaches the existence, character and attributes of God.

SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council, either provincial or general.

Key Scripture

2Ti 2:2 — "And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also."

Neh 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

Mal 2:7 — "For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts."

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Modern Corruption

The church's own school, founded so that ministers would be trained by the body they serve.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The question Kampen answered is a live one: who trains the church's ministers? Where the answer is the university, the faculty answers to the academy and the church receives whatever the academy has made. The prophets placed the duty on the ministry itself: “the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7).

The principle to recover is that theological education is an act of the church, governed by its confession and accountable to its assemblies. Kampen's founders were poor men with no endowment, and they built the school because they would not hand their pulpits to teachers the churches could not discipline.

Usage

"“who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — the reason for the school."

"“gave the sense” (Neh 8:8) — exposition as the minister's craft."

"“by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince” (Tit 1:9) — the aim of the curriculum."
